extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science and theoretical physics (educated general readers and scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for constructing and judging physical/conceptual models (atoms, ether, motion) — focusing on when hypotheses are justified, how to treat conceptual constructs, and how to avoid metaphysical overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of hypotheses by descriptive power
rubrics_metrics.description: We have a logical right to postulate laws (e.g., about atoms) when those laws, applied to large groups, enable us to describe with very great accuracy what occurs in phenomenal bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses are justified instrumentally: postulate them when they allow construction of routines of sense-impression (accurate descriptions/predictions). Do not assert metaphysical reality for a hypothesis merely because it is a useful symbol unless it is required to summarise perceptual experience without contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer an unchanging substratum from sameness of impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not follow of logical necessity that sameness of sense-impressions at different times implies the same underlying thing (substratum); permanence may lie in the grouping of impressions rather than an imperceptible substratum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use perceptual examples (e.g., waves retaining form while substratum changes) to test inferences from repeated perceptions to metaphysical permanence; be open to alternative hypotheses that explain observed sameness without positing identical underlying entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating properties (hardness, impenetrability, indestructibility) as necessary attributes of atoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes like indestructibility, impenetrability, hardness are useful hypotheses to elucidate physical/chemical properties but are not logically necessary conceptions of atoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise these attributes as model choices that may simplify description; consider alternative conceptions (e.g., penetrable atoms, varying substrata) that could equally account for phenomena. Do not project such attributes into reality without empirical necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conceptual matter from metaphysical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual matter consists of geometrical ideals endowed with relative positions, velocities, and accelerations — a symbolic shorthand for describing sense-impressions — distinct from metaphysical notions of matter as substratum, that which fills space, or that which is heavy/hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state when 'matter' is being used as a conceptual/symbolic tool versus a metaphysical claim; maintain this distinction in argumentation and avoid conflating the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as description of perceptual experience using conceptual shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Science should be confined to the field of logical inference: describing sense-impressions and their correlations by conceptual shorthand (ideal limits, geometrical ideals) rather than asserting metaphysical entities beyond perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use idealised constructs to summarise and predict perceptual data, but refrain from asserting their phenomenal existence unless required by and consistent with perceptual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simplifying conceptual bases that resume phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: A reduction (e.g., of matter to ether in motion) is valuable if it immensely simplifies symbolic description of the phenomenal universe by using a single medium's motions to describe multiple sense-impressions (hardness, weight, colour, temperature, cohesion, chemical constitution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and favour conceptual unifications that improve descriptive economy and explanatory reach, but remain cautious about projecting unified constructs into perceived reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat idealised limits (perfect fluid, perfect jelly, rigid body) as conceptual tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Incompressible/perfect-fluid/perfect-jelly/rigid-body are conceptual limits reached by carrying processes in conception; they are not exact perceptual equivalents but useful idealisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such ideal limits to frame theory and derive consequences, remembering they are relative and approximate compared to actual perceptual substances (e.g., water, jelly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile conflicting conceptual models when used together
rubrics_metrics.description: When different conceptions of the same medium (e.g., ether as perfect fluid vs. perfect jelly) are useful for different phenomena, seek a wider conception that can resume both phases without logical contradiction in investigations that require both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid slapdash mixing of incompatible models; attempt to formulate a unifying framework (e.g., viscosity spectrum, turbulence stiffening) or specify domain-limits where each model applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain macroscopic properties by types of motion (motion-stiffening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of motion (e.g., spinning elements, vortex-rings, gyrostatic effects) can 'stiffen' a medium and produce phenomena analogous to hardness, resistance, and individuality of atoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate dynamical mechanisms (vortex-rings, ether-squirts, turbulence) as ways to generate observed properties rather than positing intrinsic material qualities; use mechanical analogies and examples (spinning-top, smoke-rings) to assess plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses may be validated by descriptive scope without answering ontological origins
rubrics_metrics.description: A model (e.g., ether-squirt atom) need not explain where the ether comes from to be valid as a conceptual mechanism — it is justified if it enables resumption of perceptual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow pragmatic acceptance of models that increase descriptive/explanatory power even if they leave deeper ontological questions open, but mark those open questions as separate (not required for model utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical speculation that contradicts perceptual experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Projecting conceptions into realities beyond perception often contradicts perceptual experience; such metaphysical assertions are at best dogmas and at worst inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parables (e.g., the flounder) to show the absurdity of projecting inaccessible directions/dimensions; keep metaphysical excursions tentative and check their empirical consequences against perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical rigor as a safeguard for higher-dimensional or abstract speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher-dimensional conceptions can be legitimately explored, but they require necessary mathematical equipment to prevent over-light-hearted metaphysical excursions; if they translate back without contradiction, they may be scientifically useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require precise mathematical formulation (citing Riemann, Helmholtz, Beltrami, Clifford) for claims about higher-dimensional spaces; check consequences against perceptual data before granting physical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model acceptance requires wide-ranging descriptive power matching perceptual experience
rubrics_metrics.description: No model for the prime-atom (e.g., vortex-atom, ether-squirt) should be accepted unless it has been shown to describe perceptual experience so widely and accurately that it passes from imagination into scientific acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand empirical breadth: a successful model must account for diverse phenomena (gravitation, cohesion, light, electro-magnetism, chemical action) and not merely be suggestive or mathematically elegant.
